page_title: Get better at programming by learning how things work

sources.entry: Get better at programming by learning how things work

summary.title: Get better at programming by learning how things work
summary.one_liner: Improve as a programmer by noticing when your mental model of a system is wrong, turning confusion into specific questions, and testing answers by writing code or experiments.
keywords: connect new facts to existing knowledge
takeaways: Bugs that persist often signal a gap in your mental model of how a system works; learn to recognize that feeling of confusion.
Turn vague confusion into specific factual questions, find answers, then test them by writing a program.
Ask yes/no questions to check your understanding and avoid long explanations of things you already know.
Use experiments on your computer to answer questions the documentation does not address.
Connect new facts to what you already know (e.g. strings in memory, emoji byte sizes) so they stick, and be aware of what you still don't understand.
summary.summary: This is a personal blog essay by Julia Evans arguing that programmers improve by learning how the systems they use actually work, rather than relying only on abstractions. It gives examples across frontend JavaScript, CSS and systems programming, and describes a loop of noticing confusion, breaking it into factual questions, finding answers and testing them in code. It also covers yes/no questions as a way to get information from other people and running experiments to answer questions about the computer. The post ends by encouraging readers to be aware of their own knowledge gaps.
